newsitem.title: USA: New company becomes gum shoe of Silicon Alley.
newsitem.headline: New company becomes gum shoe of Silicon Alley.

text.p: How do you make money in an industry dominated by high-tech start ups?

One small publishing company is taking a decidedly low-tech approach, using tried-and-true gum-shoe reporting to cover New York's Silicon Alley and provide rich venture capitalists with valuable information about fledgling companies.

The firm, AlleyCat Information Services Inc., was started last year by two freelance journalists, Publisher Janet Stites and Editor-in-Chief Anna Wheatley. With savings, capital from friends and family and elbow grease, they began a newsletter covering the electronic frontier in Downtown New York City.
They have a big vision to become a kind of meeting-house where Internet, software and multimedia start-ups in New York can be joined with investors looking to place seed money in the field.
"We want to be at the nexus between start-ups and investors, where we can find information and channel it into the investment commmunity and generate revenue off that information," Wheatley said.

"Alley Cat News" is their first product -- a high-priced newsletter (subscriptions start at $850 a year), with articles about start-ups that have succeeded and failed and larger industry think pieces. Subscribers include brokerage firms, investment bankers, banks and venture firms, with notable interest from overseas, they said.

Although Stites said the venture is running break-even after six months, both take no salary, ploughing everything back into the business. This is known as sweat equity -- a mode that can continue as long as your capital and credit cards hold out.

The early success of the venture -- it's creating a buzz in Silicon Alley and among tech investors -- highlights the growing importance of new media in New York and the need among investors to find out about small companies ignored by large publications.

In the fast-growing and crash-and-burn high-tech industry, companies haved formed and gone public even before they had revenues or earnings. Investors gambled on the promise of their technology. Some have succeeded. Others have failed.

"When the Web hit, we knew this would be really valuable information for investors," Wheatley said. "Companies were incorporating and then having IPOs within 9 months so the need of investors to know about them when they were forming was very important."
Plus, she added, "no one was out there doing it yet."

Their first issue appeared in October 1996 and they took it monthly starting in January. They marketed at venture capital conferences and now have a print run of 3,000, although only a portion -- they won't say how many -- are subscribers. They have hired a marketing firm to convert the rest.

Asked why they decided on an ink-and-paper approach to an industry enamoured of the latest high-tech delivery vehicle, Wheatley said they wanted people to be able to read the publication wherever they were.

"The last thing these investment bankers want to do is read something else on their screens -- they're looking at their screens all day long," she said. Plus a newsletter was more appropriate for the longer pieces they write.

Both have a background in the field, having been associated with the futuristic science magazine OMNI and worked at the New York research firm Jupiter Communications, which provides reports and consulting on high-tech and telecommunications industries.

They also view the newsletter as an early component of the business. They deliver news bulletins by email, plan a database of information about Silicon Alley companies, and are setting up an email discussion group so investors can share information about one another and interact with start-ups.
To get all the services plus the newsletter costs $1,750 a year.

Due to their contacts with venture capitalists, they have received some interest in their own company, which they seem to be weighing. Strategic alliances with other publishers might also be a more attractive option, Stites said. Advertisers have also sounded them out.

So far they want to keep things under their own control rather than give a stake away. But they also recognise that they need to keep things apace and be prepared if a bigger competitor enters the field.

"One of the advantages is that we're not attached to anything, to one way of doing things, like a big company would be. That gives us an advantage and people are supportive because of that," Stites said.
